articles.title: 175 years of putting customers first
articles.summary: One hundred seventy-five years is an extraordinary milestone, and one that carries both pride and responsibility. Very few institutions have had the privilege of serving generations of Filipinos…

blocks.text: One hundred seventy-five years is an extraordinary milestone, and one that carries both pride and responsibility. Very few institutions have had the privilege of serving generations of Filipinos through life’s most important moments, helping them save, build businesses, and achieve their dreams.

For BPI, our anniversary is more than a celebration of longevity. It is an opportunity to reflect on a simple question: what allows an institution to remain relevant for nearly two centuries? Many would point to innovation. Others would point to resilience. I believe it begins with something even simpler: an unwavering focus on the customer.

When BPI was established in 1851, the Philippines looked very different. Banking was conducted through ledgers, handwritten records, and face-to-face conversations. Since then, we've witnessed enormous changes—not only in banking, but in the country itself.

Yet despite all those changes, one truth has remained constant: people don’t aspire for financial products. They aspire for what those products make possible — starting a business, buying a home, educating their children, recovering from setbacks, and building a more secure future. Understanding that difference has shaped BPI for 175 years. It continues to shape how we serve our customers today.
That's why one of the things I often tell our teams is this: People don't really want a bank. They want a simpler, better life. That perspective has shaped every major chapter of BPI's history.

When we introduced modern banking to the Philippines, it wasn't simply about bringing new financial services to the country. It was about helping Filipinos participate in a growing economy. When we pioneered ATM banking, the goal wasn't to showcase new technology. It was to give customers access to their money beyond traditional banking hours. When we embraced digital banking, the objective wasn't to become more digital for its own sake. It was to make banking faster, more convenient, and more accessible. Today, that same thinking guides our investments in agency banking, allowing us to bring banking services closer to communities where convenience means something different for every customer.

Looking back, it's easy to celebrate these milestones as moments of innovation. I see them differently. They are moments of listening. Each innovation began with the same question: How can we make life better for our customers?
The answers have changed over 175 years. The question never has. That mindset has become even more important today.

Artificial intelligence is transforming industries. Digital payments happen in seconds. Financial services are becoming increasingly connected. These advances are exciting, and they hold tremendous promise for expanding financial inclusion and improving customer experiences. But technology alone does not create meaningful innovation. Innovation begins with understanding people. Technology is an enabler. Trust is the foundation.
The institutions that will thrive in the future won't necessarily be those with the newest technology. They will be those that know their customers best and continuously evolve alongside them.
But customer obsession isn't built through strategy alone. It's brought to life by people.

For 175 years, generations of BPI employees have been the face of that commitment. Every account we open, every loan we approve, every payment we process, every investment we recommend, every digital solution we build, and every concern we resolve is more than a banking transaction. It is an opportunity to make someone's life a little easier, a little better, and a little more secure.

Looking ahead, I have no doubt that banking will continue to evolve. The possibilities are immense. But I also believe that the next breakthrough in banking won't simply come from a new technology. It will come from listening more closely, understanding more deeply, and responding more thoughtfully to the people we serve.
As we celebrate BPI's 175th anniversary, we're proud of the milestones we've achieved. More importantly, we're grateful for the trust that generations of Filipinos have placed in us.

That trust has been our greatest privilege. It has also been our greatest responsibility. And it is why, after 175 years, our most enduring competitive advantage isn't simply our history. It is our commitment to continuously earning the right to serve our customers, today and for generations to come. In doing so, we fulfill our purpose of building a better Philippines—one family, one community at a time.

articles.title: Time to shine for Gilas locals
articles.summary: EDITORS DESK Today, Aug. 28, 2026, Gilas Pilipinas makes a crucial home stand against the visiting Jordan team at the Mall of Asia Arena in Pasay City. Two days later, it’s Gilas versus Iran. On the…

blocks.text: EDITORS DESK
Today, Aug. 28, 2026, Gilas Pilipinas makes a crucial home stand against the visiting Jordan team at the Mall of Asia Arena in Pasay City.
Two days later, it’s Gilas versus Iran.

On the surface, it is all about earning a spot in the 2027 FIBA World Cup set in Qatar. There is also the bigger goal, with the centerpiece event awarding top finishers from each continent a precious ticket to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

While it is paramount that the Nationals be able to secure more victories to better their 2-4 win-loss record and get a fighting chance in their group come two more windows in November and February of next year, there lies a problem that is wrapped like a gift for the future of our national team.
No Justin Brownlee, no Bennie Boatwright, no Ange Kouame, no Jordan Clarkson.

While it holds true value that these naturalized players offer the firepower, ceiling, the tenacity, and steely nerves for our team on any given situation, this showcase against the Middle East giants could give this basketball-crazed country a glimpse of future in its most bare, natural, all-Filipino form.
Time is now for the local cast to step up and show the crowd the resolve they have in critical situation.
The Nationals are playing the August window without their most dependable and consistent player in Justin Brownlee.
Brownlee, who was supposed to make his comeback after sustaining a myriad of injuries from his hamstring to his knees, won't be able to suit up for Gilas this weekend as he recovers in the US.
The 38-year-old forward was also absent when the national team played New Zealand and Australia last July.

Former San Miguel import Bennie Boatwright was a candidate to become a naturalized Filipino, but his papers won't make it in time with his documents now stuck in the Senate that is busy handling the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Ange Kouame could have been someone to be tapped in, but the 6-foot-10 center is still under his basketball contract in France.
Jordan Clarkson was floated, but there is so much needed to get his services as he is a certified NBA star.

These challenges pose a big threat to our national team's ambition of advancing to the World Cup, and these are the same hurdles the Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas should face when another all-Filipino crew plunges into action in the Asian Games where the country is the defending men's champion.
Without them, it sounds scary. But without them opens up the opportunity for the locals to further shine.

Minutes will be diverted to young guns Carl Tamayo, Kevin Quiambao and Dwight Ramos. Crucial shots could be handed to CJ Perez or Scottie Thompson. Defense is as agile and tall with Kai Sotto and June Mar Fajardo manning the paint.
When one is absent, everyone steps forward.
And this could be the stage of proving each one's worth when everything is on the line.
Above all, the crowd will be satisfied: this is all-Filipino.
(Ramon Rafael Bonilla is the editor of Manila Bulletin's Sports section.)

articles.title: Beyond disaster response: Redefining resilience
articles.summary: METRO MATTERS Every year, cities from all across the country face the challenge of mitigating disaster risks amid worsening global climate conditions. It is my mandate as mayor of the City of San…

blocks.text: METRO MATTERS

Every year, cities from all across the country face the challenge of mitigating disaster risks amid worsening global climate conditions. It is my mandate as mayor of the City of San Juan, president of the Metro Manila Council, and national president of the League of Cities of the Philippines to maximize government efforts to partner with the private sector to ensure the safety of Filipinos.

San Juan City is not exempt from the effects of these natural calamities as heavy rains continue to pour especially during the Southwest monsoon season. Yet despite the heavy downpour from Aug. 5 to 9, our preparations helped keep flooding in the city to a minimum, with no reported evacuations even in our low-lying areas.

On Aug. 10, when the rain continued to pour heavily and persistently, flood levels rose, but they were no longer as high as what we experienced in the past. We have seen significant improvements, but we also recognize the work that still needs to be done.
This was not the result of a single intervention. It was the product of months of dredging, sustained drainage cleaning and waste management programs all throughout the city.

We launched our search for the Cleanest Barangay, with the winner receiving ₱200,000, the 1st runner-up receiving ₱100,000 and the 2nd runner-up receiving ₱50,000, to encourage communities to work together and strengthen their environmental awareness and initiatives. We also amended our local ordinance to increase the penalty for improper waste disposal to ₱5,000, regardless of whether it is a first, second or third offense, as a deterrent. Through a resolution of the Metro Manila Council, we have encouraged similar efforts across the National Capital Region. But no government program can succeed without the discipline and genuine sense of stewardship of our communities. We are fortunate to have citizens who heed our calls and actively help us keep our waterways clean.

Still, preparation for the next disaster cannot stop with immediate response and routine maintenance. We must also address the long-term causes that contribute to flooding. Waste management is one of these challenges. As our cities continue to grow, we need solutions that are sustainable.

In my capacity as president of the Metro Manila Council, I have welcomed dialogues on alternative waste management methods, including the possibility of converting waste to energy. We are currently reviewing proposals and studying this technology to determine how it can be responsibly and effectively adapted to our cities’ needs.
Building resilience means investing not only in infrastructure, but also in our people and our environment.

Under our Makabagong San Juan administration, we continue to pursue projects to strengthen the city’s long-term flood resilience. We are constructing a new pumping station along F. Manalo Street in Barangay Batis and another one near the San Juan River. We have also purchased mobile pumps that can be deployed to different locations depending on necessity.

With the help of the national government, we are improving our drainage systems in various barangays. I have also met with my colleagues from other local government units in Metro Manila to discuss how we can consolidate our efforts as an interconnected region, because disaster preparedness and response cannot stop at city boundaries.
Resilience must also begin at home.

Last Aug. 12, we started distributing Emergency Go Bags to District 1 barangays, with District 2 following the day after. Each Go Bag contains basic survival items such as a hard hat, waterproof poncho, rechargeable flashlight, power bank, basic disaster preparedness handbook, and first aid kit. Our goal is to provide these to all 45,000 San Juan households by the first quarter of 2027. We continue to strengthen disaster preparedness in San Juan, making it a constant part of how we protect our communities, not just a response when a storm is approaching.

We are privileged to have a strong and mutually beneficial partnership with the private sector. I want to express my gratitude to Mr. Ramon Ang and San Miguel Corporation for their assistance in dredging the San Juan River, Maytunas Creek, and Ermitaño Creek at no cost to the city under Oplan Kontra Baha of our Bagong Pilipinas Administration. Our continued partnership with SMC, together with the support of the national government and the cooperation of our local communities, proves that we can better serve our people when we work hand-in-hand.

The challenges brought about by climate change remind us that resilience cannot be built by one city or one institution alone. It requires sustained preparation, responsible citizenship, strong partnerships, and investments that will protect our communities for years to come. This is the responsibility we share as local governments: to prepare before disaster strikes, protect our people when it does, and build a nation where no Filipino is left behind.

articles.title: Five were wise
articles.summary: REFLECTIONS TODAY Jesus’ question, “Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant?” in the parable of the Faithful Servant (Mt 24:45), should now be read, “Who then is the faithful and wise virgin?”…

blocks.text: REFLECTIONS TODAY

Jesus’ question, “Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant?” in the parable of the Faithful Servant (Mt 24:45), should now be read, “Who then is the faithful and wise virgin?” Going by the parable, the wise virgins are those whose eyes are open to what is yet to come; they do not simply live for the day. Christ will return and ask us for an accounting of our life.

The wise prepare for it beforehand. Here, they are symbolized by the five virgins who provide themselves with enough oil. The foolish are those who do not think of the future, do not prepare for it, and miss opportunities given them. They think that conversion is always possible at the last moment, or that they can always rely on others to rescue them from their predicament. Even as we do not know the day or the hour when we will meet the Lord, so we must always be prepared.

We cannot borrow someone else’s faith or grace at the last minute; we must cultivate our own. Like the wise virgins, we must have the foresight to bring extra oil—with spiritual readiness by living in the state of grace, continually nurturing our relationship with God through prayer, the sacraments, and acts of love and charity. We must ditch lethargy, laziness, and indifference so that we will not be found wanting when we face the Lord.
Gospel • Matthew 25:1-13

Jesus told his disciples this parable: “The Kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish and five were wise. The foolish ones, when taking their lamps, brought no oil with them, but the wise brought flasks of oil with their lamps. Since the bridegroom was long delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep.

“At midnight, there was a cry, ‘Behold, the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!’ Then all those virgins got up and trimmed their lamps. The foolish ones said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ But the wise ones replied, ‘No, for there may not be enough for us and you. Go instead to the merchants and buy some for yourselves.’ While they went off to buy it, the bridegroom came and those who were ready went into the wedding feast with him. Then the door was locked. Afterwards the other virgins came and said, ‘Lord, Lord, open the door for us!’ But he said in reply, ‘Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.’ Therefore, stay awake, for you know neither the day nor the hour.”
Source: “365 Days with the Lord 2026,” St. Paul’s, 7708 St. Paul Rd., SAV, Makati City (Phils.); Tel.: 632-895-9701; E-mail: [email protected]; Website: http://www.stpauls.ph.

articles.title: A supportive LGU is key to a thriving agriculture industry
articles.summary: AVANT GARDENER What happens when an NGO’s project ends? If done well, it continues even without the organization’s supervision. I was invited to the End-of-Project Workshop of the International…

blocks.text: AVANT GARDENER
What happens when an NGO’s project ends? If done well, it continues even without the organization’s supervision.

I was invited to the End-of-Project Workshop of the International Institute for Rural Reconstruction’s (IIRR) and the International Development Research Centre’s AQUADAPT project, which supports the small farmer’s adoption of nature-based aquaculture as an additional source of income in the Philippines and in Cambodia.

You’ll notice that I’ve been writing a lot about IIRR. Before this, all of it came from a trip to Guinayangan, Quezon, upon the invitation of IIRR’s Senior Asia Program Advisor Dr. Julian Gonsalves, who I met at the International Plant Breeding Conference in celebration of UPLB’s Institute of Plant Breeding’s 50th Anniversary at the Manila Hotel in 2025.
I’ve been interested in IIRR’s work because it deals with factors specific to most of the Philippine agriculture landscape, i.e. small farms. In short, it works with culture and not against it.

“[The project explored] how small-scale agriculture can become a more resilient, sustainable, and viable life in options for rural communities in the face of a challenging climate," said Ermita Monville Oro, IIRR’s Acting Asia Regional Director. “Just as importantly, the project has brought attention to the critical role of women in agriculture value chains.”
What interested me most about IIRR is its insistence that the local government be involved in all their projects to ensure its continuous adoption even after the project ends.

The program included a panel with three government officials from its Philippine sites: Hon. Mayor Lovell Anne Yu-Castro of Alangalang, Leyte; Municipal Agriculture Officer of Guniyangan, Quezon William Lopez Jr.; and Municipal Agriculture Officer of Hingyon, Ifugao Andy Dimoc, who all answered the question that, given the end of the project, “What would be needed to make this approach sustainable at the local level?”
Yu-Castro discussed how a lawmaker can implement a program past their term by using AQUADAPT as an example.

“We have seen the success stories of our farmers. This project is evidence based,” she said in Taglish. “What I'm thinking is for us to institutionalize AQUADAPT implementation in our programs, in our PPAs (Public-Private Partnerships). We will be institutionalizing the AQUADAPT budgeting, the program implementation in our agricultural development programs… We will make it an ordinance so that even with the change in local officials, the support for AQUADAPT will stay. It will always be supported because this program will be institutionalized in Alangalang. We’re going to do that with the help of IIRR and our representative from MAO.”

Dimoc agreed, adding that participant ownership and a definite delineation of responsibilities among partner farmers and organizations are also important. “I think that this is really needed, especially if we are going to use the government funds in all these nature-based solutions programs. And those ordinances should have… funds their own. In our (area), we have a memorandum of agreement with our partner organizations, with our farmers, so that at least this is binding to both parties, I think, because they do this and responsibilities will be spelled out, so they know what are their duties and responsibilities, and also on our end, we know also our duties and responsibilities as partner LGUs,” he said.

Lopez, whose work in Guinayangan I will be writing about in a later column, echoed Yu-Castro’s sentiment by emphasizing the importance of a mayor who is heavily invested in the growth of their municipality’s various agriculture industries.

“To sustain this program, we are planning to enhance the nursery and we will make it a learning site so that the other aquaculture farmers, they will learn in our local municipality,” he said, explaining that in Gunayangan, LGU support came in the form of two fishery technicians for program monitoring and evaluation, the allotment of part of the annual budget to the development of the program, the enhancement of their municipal hatchery, and the development of an organic tilapia feed production program.

“We are planning to provide an adequate source of water for the rice-tilapia-based aquaculture [in coordination with the] National Irrigation Association,” he added. “We also intensified the seaboard patrolling, since we have 15 barangays coastal areas. Before, we were focused on marine monitoring for illegal fishing, but because of the AQUADAPT, we've also monitored the mangrove areas and the conservation of the species.”

The panel’s experiences show that local government cooperation and support is an extremely important factor in determining the longevity and continuation of NGO-led small-scale farmer programs, especially after these programs end. After all, the proof of an NGO’s effectiveness is when a community doesn’t need them anymore.

articles.title: ₱7.2-trillion test: Can the House deliver an honest 2027 budget?
articles.summary: The filing of the proposed ₱7.2-trillion 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB), or House Bill No. 10858, presents the House of Representatives with more than another annual budget exercise. It is a…

blocks.text: The filing of the proposed ₱7.2-trillion 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB), or House Bill No. 10858, presents the House of Representatives with more than another annual budget exercise. It is a test of whether Congress has learned the painful lessons of the 2025 budget and the flood-control scandal—and whether it is prepared to restore public trust.

House Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Rep. Mikaela Angela “Mika” Suansing (1st District, Nueva Ecija) said the House may realign allocations among sectors and agencies as it sees fit. There is nothing inherently wrong with realignment. Congress has the constitutional authority and responsibility to scrutinize the executive’s proposed spending budget and improve it.
But the question is: Improve it for whom?

As congressmen deliberate on the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program, they must keep in mind that the ₱7.2-trillion budget is taxpayers’ money. Every peso carries the labor of a worker, the sacrifice of a family, the enterprise of a business, and the hopes of a citizen.
Therefore, the ₱7.2 trillion must serve the Filipino people—not political allies, favored districts, contractors, or private interests.

The proposed budget puts substantial resources into education, public works, health, local government, national defense, transportation, agriculture, social welfare and state universities. These allocations should translate into better schools, accessible health care, safer communities, productive farms, reliable infrastructure, and genuine opportunities for ordinary Filipinos.

The House must therefore treat every proposed realignment with suspicion—not because every amendment is corrupt, but because the experience of the 2025 budget demonstrated how opaque amendments can become fertile ground for abuse.

The flood-control controversy is a warning that Congress cannot afford to ignore. Senate investigations in 2025 uncovered allegations involving questionable, failed, and even “ghost” projects, while lawmakers themselves raised concerns over congressional insertions. Sen. Panfilo Lacson said congressional amendments are not necessarily illegal, but warned that large individual insertions can undermine properly planned government programs.

More troubling is the so-called “small committee,” where substantial changes to the budget could be made behind closed doors. Reports on the 2025 process described how this mechanism became another point at which alleged insertions could occur.
This is where the House must draw a bright and clear line.
No secret budget. No mystery amendments. No anonymous insertions. No political pork disguised as public spending.

If a lawmaker proposes moving billions of pesos from one agency or program to another, the public deserves to know who proposed it, why it was proposed, what project or program will receive the money, and what technical and fiscal basis supports the change.

Budget deliberations, including amendments and realignments, should be conducted in public through the appropriate House committees—or, when necessary, the plenary. The public should not have to rely on leaks, insiders, or investigations years later to discover where their money went.
Yes, open deliberations may take longer. But democracy is not supposed to be optimized for speed at the expense of accountability.
The House has an opportunity to make the 2027 national budget a genuine instrument of national development and social justice—from the poorest Filipino to the wealthiest.
The challenge is simple but profound: Will Congress merely pass the biggest budget in Philippine history—or will it produce one worthy of the people who pay for it?
The answer should be an honest-to-goodness budget, forged in the full light of day.

articles.title: NNIC turning 2
articles.summary: A little over two weeks from now, San Miguel Corp. (SMC) Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Ramon “RSA” S. Ang and his New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC) team will be celebrating their second year of…

blocks.text: A little over two weeks from now, San Miguel Corp. (SMC) Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Ramon “RSA” S. Ang and his New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC) team will be celebrating their second year of managing and upgrading the country’s premier airport.

As the saying goes: time flies when you’re engrossed, immersed, and focused on the task at hand—providing ease and comfort for both inbound and outbound passengers, as well as welcoming relatives and well-wishers.

Even before turning two this Sept. 14, NNIC (as of end-July this year) has already remitted some ₱78 billion, representing the national government’s 82.16 percent revenue share. That amount includes the ₱30 billion upfront payment.
Yes, Virginia, the renovations, changes, and upgrades at NAIA have reached a fever pitch, with the NNIC team successfully navigating and managing active operational constraints.

I saw this firsthand when I joined former Transportation Secretary and newly elected SMC independent board director Jaime “JJB” J. Bautista for a special tour showcasing the progress of the Terminal 3 renovations.

As a passenger, it was satisfying—delightful, even—to see the improvements NNIC has undertaken at the multi-level terminal, bringing significant upgrades to dining, boarding bridges, and passenger lounges.
Under the skillful management of NNIC Vice President for Commercial Operations Cecile Ang, underused spaces were converted into comfortable dining and retail hubs.

For this foodie, it’s comforting to note the wide variety of local and international dining options available in International Departures and at the Tambayan Food Hall, a waiting area for welcomers and well-wishers.
Shake Shack, Wildflour, Cibo, Conti's, Ramen Nagi, Lechon Diva, Starbucks Reserve, and the highly sought-after Estrel’s Specialty Bakeshop are among the notable additions.

I heard that Estrel’s business is thriving in T3, as folks in the southern part of the metropolis no longer have to traverse chaotic roads and endure the long drive to Quezon City for its caramel-iced chiffon cake, which, I believe, gives Hizon’s a real run for its money (and its cake).

Taking cognizance of the vital role played by the country’s unsung heroes, our overseas Filipino workers, whose dollar remittances pump up our current account position—NNIC has allocated a special lounge for them with ample seating, a relaxing ambiance, phone-charging stations, and, of course, free food and drinks.

The OFW Lounge is operated by the Department of Migrant Workers through its attached agency, the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA), which protects and promotes the well-being of OFWs and their families. Earmarking ₱10 million a month for maintenance, the lounge can accommodate 216 passengers.

But wait, Virginia, there’s more! For those with delayed flights, sleeping quarters are available with a capacity for 26 people—14 for men and 12 for women—replete with toiletry kits and shower rooms for freshening up.

Business-class passengers, on the other hand, can while away the time at the First Meridian Lounge. This 2,600-square-meter shared premium facility serves Emirates, Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines, Thai Airways, KLM, and Vietnam Airlines. It features a full-service bar, hot and cold buffets, a bakery section, a playroom, and an infant care section.
According to a Meridian staff member, the virtual golf simulator is the most popular amenity and is almost always booked.

Beyond terminal aesthetics, ongoing and pipeline project upgrades include the phased rehabilitation of passenger boarding bridges and fixed bridges, the installation of new escalators, and the construction of Terminal 5—set for completion around 2028—which will be dedicated to Philippine Airlines and AirAsia domestic operations.

Exploring the expanse of the 183,000-square-meter T3 complex, I observed an aura of delight and satisfaction from JJB and the NNIC team. In 2025, UK-based Project Finance International recognized the long-overdue rehabilitation of the country’s premier airport through a public-private partnership, naming it the “Transport Deal Award of the Year.”
Although much remains to be done, NAIA T3 has earned its mark and is now ranked 7th globally for having the highest number of food and beverage outlets per million passengers.
Way to go, NNIC! A salute to RSA and your team.
Talk back to me at [email protected]

articles.title: Optimus Prime and Eeyore voice actor Peter Cullen dies
articles.summary: Cullen voiced the heroic Optimus Prime in the Transformers TV series and then the Hollywood films.

blocks.text: His Optimus Prime voice was inspired by his older brother, a decorated US Marine and Vietnam War veteran, who suggested he should play the character as "a real hero, don't be a Hollywood hero".
"He said, 'Don't go yelling and screaming. He's strong enough to be gentle.'
"And that resonated with me, and I could hear his voice all the way to the audition. When he drops down, when he gets serious, is where I found Optimus Prime."
Cullen gave his brother a cut of the wages he received for playing Optimus Prime until his death.

The actor's performance as the character earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for outstanding performer in an animated programme in 2011, and he was honoured with a lifetime achievement award at the Children's & Family Emmy Awards in 2023.

Cullen's other roles included Monterey Jack in Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, and he voiced characters in 1980s and 90s animated series including Spider-Man, Donkey Kong, Alvin & the Chipmunks, Dungeons & Dragons, My Little Pony, Duck Tales and Gummi Bears.

articles.title: UP needs fresh funding for NOAH
articles.summary: The University of the Philippines is seeking fresh funding in the 2027 national budget for Project NOAH, the core component of the UP Resilience Institute responsible for developing hazard maps that…

blocks.text: The UPRI received P1 billion this week from the Department of Budget and Management for Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards). It was earmarked in the 2026 budget after the government cut P255 billion from the Department of Public Works and Highways budget in the aftermath of the flood control scandal.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The University of the Philippines is seeking fresh funding in the 2027 national budget for Project NOAH, the core component of the UP Resilience Institute responsible for developing hazard maps that policymakers and the public use to plan for weather events.

The UPRI received P1 billion this week from the Department of Budget and Management for Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards). It was earmarked in the 2026 budget after the government cut P255 billion from the Department of Public Works and Highways budget in the aftermath of the flood control scandal.
The UPRI will use the mon- ey to upgrade its equipment, enhance hazard maps and fund research endeavors.
But the 2027 National Ex- penditure Program, for now, contains no new money for Project NOAH
The university pointed out that its funding in the 2026 budget was finalized only uring the bicameral conference committee.
UPRI executive director Mahar Lagmay said the P1 billion is “a good start,” but is not enough to execute all the plans they have in mind.
However, it’s a marked improvement from 2017 when NOAH was transferred to the UPRI.

Project NOAH had an annual budget of only over P30 million at the time, which it used to help cities craft their flood control master plans.With the huge increase in NOAH’s budget, Lagmay lai out the UPRI’s priority spending areas: high-resolution mapping of major river basins, support for the government’s Oplan Kontra Baha, simulation of major detention basins, drone surveys with state colleges and universities, native-tree mapping, sediment erosion and delivery assessment, mapping hidden waterways, promotion of nature-based solutions and artificial intel- ligence for disaster management.

articles.title: DepEd backs school safety bill amid shootings
articles.summary: Amid recent shooting incidents and other security concerns in schools, Education Secretary Sonny Angara yesterday expressed his support for the passage of the Comprehensive School Safety Act that…

blocks.text: This file photo shows a facade of the Department of Education.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Amid recent shooting incidents and other security concerns in schools, Education Secretary Sonny Angara yesterday expressed his support for the passage of the Comprehensive School Safety Act that gives priority to school safety and well-being of learners.
The Department of Education (DepEd) said Angara showed his support to Sen. Bam Aquino at the Senate on Wednesday as the senator proposed the Comprehensive School Safety Act.
The bill seeks to institutionalize DepEd’s ongoing learner protection initiatives into permanent law, ensuring that critical safety protocols remain funded and sustained.
The legislative push follows nationwide concerns after shooting incidents at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban and the Ateneo de Zamboanga University.
The proposed Comprehensive School Safety Act establishes a three-pillar framework: prevention, response and recovery.
Under prevention, the bill mandates risk identification and safety training for parents, teachers and student leaders.
Response outlines emergency protocols, communication networks, active attack safety drills and coordination with authorities.
The recovery phase ensures psychosocial support, trauma-informed care and structured return-to-school plans.
The DepEd is expediting the recruitment of 10,000 school counselor associates nationwide, aiming to deploy them by year-end.
La Salle security
A student’s message on an online group chat with fellow students that he is a shooter disrupted classes at La Salle Greenhills in Mandaluyong City yesterday.

In a Facebook post, the school aid classes from preschool to Grade 12, including International Baccalaureate and Alternative Education programs, were conducted online as a precautionary measure. – Emmanuel Tupas

articles.title: Sweeping DPWH budget reforms set
articles.summary: There will be a sweeping overhaul in the budget submission process of the Department of Public Works and Highways, whose total project count for next year will be slashed by more than half, DPWH…

blocks.text: DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon also warned DPWH district engineers (DEs) that signing off on unvetted or “defective, anomalous” projects could land them in jail.
DPWH via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — There will be a sweeping overhaul in the budget submission process of the Department of Public Works and Highways, whose total project count for next year will be slashed by more than half, DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said yesterday.
Dizon also warned DPWH district engineers (DEs) that signing off on unvetted or “defective, anomalous” projects could land them in jail.

Highlighting a complete departure from “old budget habits” that allowed billions in public funds to be squandered on poorly planned infrastructure projects, Dizon said the DPWH is imposing a strict “no plan, no budget” policy across all regional and district offices.
“The old ways of budgeting are over,” he told reporters yesterday during his inspection of flood control and infrastructure projects at the EDSA Balintawak Cloverleaf area in Quezon City.

“We no longer accept project entries that consist of just a line-item title and a price tag. Projects must originate from community needs and satisfy complete prerequisite engineering requirements before entering the budget.”

Under the newly instituted accountability framework, DEs are required to personally sign certification documents guaranteeing that submitted projects have secured right-of-way acquisitions, detailed engineering designs and complete programs of work.
Dizon cautioned field officials against blindly approving lump-sum or unverified proposals, warning that their personal signatures will serve as primary evidence in criminal proceedings.

“If a DE signs off on a project and it turns out to be defective, anomalous, or ghost infrastructure, they are automatically held accountable,” he warned. “I will bring their signed certifications directly to the National Bureau of Investigation or the Ombudsman. It will be an open-and-shut case, and corrupt district engineers will go straight to prison.”

To enforce strict quality control and eliminate bloated, uncoordinated civil works, Dizon said the DPWH drastically pared down its project portfolio from 26,000 projects in previous budget cycles down to 11,000 highly targeted national projects.
Dizon reiterated that every approved project must carry written concurrence from the concerned local government unit to ensure alignment with local drainage and traffic master plans.
“While these reforms aren’t entirely foolproof, they create a formidable shield against the systemic corruption of the past,” Dizon added. “We will remain vigilant in guarding the public coffers.”

articles.title: P7.2 trillion budget bill for 2027 filed
articles.summary: The bill containing the government’s spending plan worth P7.2 trillion for fiscal year has been formally filed before the House of Representatives.

blocks.text: The bill serves as the legislative equivalent of the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) that Malacañang annually submits to Congress.
Philstar.com / Irra Lising
MANILA, Philippines — The bill containing the government’s spending plan worth P7.2 trillion for fiscal year has been formally filed before the House of Representatives.
House committee on appropriations chairperson Mikaela Suansing said she has formally filed House Bill 10858 or the 2027 General Appropriations Bill.
The bill serves as the legislative equivalent of the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) that Malacañang annually submits to Congress.
“We are working to ensure the careful scrutiny of the national budget for the year 2027,” Suansing said.
The House of Representatives started the committee-level budget deliberations last week.
After the committee, the bill will then be deliberated at the plenary.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) earlier said the Department of Education (P976 billion) and Department of Public Works and Highways (P644 billion) were among the agencies with the largest allocations in the proposed budget for next year.
Senate conducts budget hearing

The Senate yesterday led the Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC) hearing into the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, with economic managers and senators talking about the need to tame inflation and end corruption following the flood control mess.

Monetary and fiscal managers from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), Department of Finance, and DBM were grilled by the senators about the rising cost of living and the global headwinds – like regional wars and oil price shocks – that affect economic growth.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian questioned BSP Governor Eli Remolona about the capacity of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), which Remolona chairs, in flagging suspicious bank flows due to corruption.

Sen. Francis Pangilinan pointed toAMLC’s failure to flag Syms Construction flood control contractorSally Santos’ transaction at Landbank in cashing out an alleged P457 million kickback to dismissed district engineer Brice Hernandez, a finding of last year’s explosive Blue Ribbon flood control inquiry.

articles.title: Teachers’ group slams P3.34 billion budget cut for SUCs
articles.summary: The Alliance of Concerned Teachers yesterday condemned the P3.34-billion slash in the budget for state universities and colleges or SUCs under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), while P10.8…

blocks.text: Out of 116 SUCs nationwide, 49 will suffer direct budget slashes while seven others will receive nominal increases of less than one percent.
Ramon Efren Lazaro

MANILA, Philippines — The Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) yesterday condemned the P3.34-billion slash in the budget for state universities and colleges or SUCs under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), while P10.8 billion was allocated for confidential and intelligence funds or CIF.

In a statement, ACT chairperson Ruby Bernardo said that while the SUCs suffer budget cuts, P10.8 billion was allocated for CIFs – with P4.56 billion, or 44.9 percent of the total CIF, for the Office of the President alone.
Out of 116 SUCs nationwide, 49 will suffer direct budget slashes while seven others will receive nominal increases of less than one percent.
“The cutbacks in education are directly depriving the young Filipinos of their rights to education,” Bernardo said.

ACT said the University of the Philippines System bears the single largest budget slash, losing nearly P2.95 billion – a move that would directly cripple funding for the Philippine General Hospital, which is the country’s premier government tertiary medical facility.
Specialized institutions such as the Philippine Normal University and Polytechnic University of the Philippines also face hefty cuts with P394.9 million and P291.8 million, respectively.
ACT asked lawmakers to immediately reject all proposed budget cuts, and fully restore the P3.34-billion reduction across all 49 affected SUCs.
The teachers’ group noted that the Department of the Interior and Local Government was given a P22-billion budget increase in the NEP, of which P16 billion would go to the Philippine National Police.

articles.title: BOC chief vows zero tolerance for agri smuggling
articles.summary: Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno has assured farmers that the agency will remain relentless in its fight against agricultural smuggling, emphasizing that protecting local producers, securing…

blocks.text: Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno speaks to farmers during a recent event
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno has assured farmers that the agency will remain relentless in its fight against agricultural smuggling, emphasizing that protecting local producers, securing national borders, and ensuring proper government revenue collection are among the bureau’s top priorities.

Addressing members of the Magsasaka party-list and farmer leaders from Pampanga, Bataan, Aurora, Tarlac, Zambales, and Nueva Ecija, Nepomuceno acknowledged the damaging impact of smuggling on the livelihoods of farmers and fisherfolk across the country.

The Customs chief stressed that while the challenges confronting the agriculture sector extend beyond smuggling, the bureau remains committed to fulfilling its mandate through stronger border protection and stricter enforcement against customs fraud and illicit trade.
Nepomuceno also underscored President Marcos’ directives to strengthen revenue collection, minimize corruption, and modernize the Bureau of Customs.
He noted that the BOC has surpassed its revenue collection target by more than P11 billion, proving that reforms and efficient revenue generation can go hand in hand.

According to the commissioner, every successful effort to stop smuggling not only protects legitimate businesses and local producers but also ensures that government revenues intended for public programs and services are properly collected.
Reforms in the bureau have just started and this will be carried out over the long haul, he said.
He assured farmers of his continued support, saying he is on their side.

The gathering was attended by Magsasaka party-list chairman and former representative Argel Joseph Cabatbat, DIWA party-list chairman and former representative Michael Aglipay, Vice Mayor Allan Policarpio representing Mayor Michael Galang, and various farmer leaders from Central Luzon.

A highlight of the gathering was the approval of a motion conferring upon Nepomuceno the distinction of honorary member of Magsasaka, in recognition of his support for farmers and commitment to combating agricultural smuggling.

articles.title: Palace: No FB ban for now; Meta cooperating with government
articles.summary: The government is not banning Facebook for now, but is pushing for clearer FB rules on eliminating online content that promotes disinformation and encourages violence.

blocks.text: Palace press officer Claire Castro told a media briefing last Tuesday that the administration is open to banning Facebook and gaming applications following concerns about disinformation and the rising cases of deadly school violence.
AFP
MANILA, Philippines — The government is not banning Facebook for now, but is pushing for clearer FB rules on eliminating online content that promotes disinformation and encourages violence.

Palace press officer Claire Castro told a media briefing last Tuesday that the administration is open to banning Facebook and gaming applications following concerns about disinformation and the rising cases of deadly school violence.
The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center proposed the ban days after the shooting incident at the Ateneo de Zamboanga, which claimed the lives of two persons.
Speaking to reporters yesterday, Castro said Facebook has been responsive to the government’s efforts to immediately take down “fake news.”

“Facebook is not difficult to deal with and it doesn’t mean that if other social media platforms are not responsive, all of them would be banned. That is not what the President and our administration wants,” she said.

“But this is also a signal for other violators, especially the gaming apps that we know affect our youth and can cause violence. So that is what we want to relay because even if the President is open (to a ban), based on the latest information, our government does not have much problem with Facebook,” she added.

Castro urged other social media platforms to work with the government to prevent the spread of false information and violent content. She revealed that Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda is set to travel to Singapore to meet with regional executives of Meta and discuss ways to immediately get rid of violent and false posts.

articles.title: DILG wants PNP access to homes of legal gun owners
articles.summary: The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has proposed allowing police access to inspect homes of owners of lawfully issued firearms to check procedures for safekeeping.

blocks.text: Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla on September 1, 2025.
STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has proposed allowing police access to inspect homes of owners of lawfully issued firearms to check procedures for safekeeping.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla yesterday suggested amending guidelines on the handling of government-issued guns amid recent fatal school shooting incidents that involved such weapons.
In his proposal, Remulla said firearm owners will be informed ahead of time about the inspection and they would provide a checklist and reminders on proper safekeeping practices.
He admitted that such a proposal might “upset some people” but reminded them that owning and carrying a gun is only a privilege.
He pointed out that in both cases of the recent school shootings in Tacloban and Zamboanga, the safekeeping of the guns was not in standard procedure.
In the Tacloban incident, a policewoman owned the government-issued gun used by one of the shooters, her nephew.
Meanwhile, the guns used in the Ateneo de Zamboanga University were owned by the father of the shooter, who was a Bureau of Customs personnel.
Remulla also urged Congress to repeal Republic Act 8294 or the so-called Robin Padilla law, which reduced penalties for illegal possession of firearms and made it a bailable offense.
However, he acknowledged that the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology could need additional funds to enhance their facilities if the law is repealed.
“Loose firearms in this country are prevalent. And if we catch them, it will be non-bailable, so we will need more room in our jails,” he said.

articles.title: PH may be caught in US rivals’ ‘crosshairs’ – Tinio
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday warned that the growing US presence in the country’s military and economic assets could put the…

blocks.caption: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., left, speaks during a meeting with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, right, at the Pentagon, Monday, July 21, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday warned that the growing US presence in the country’s military and economic assets could put the Philippines in the “crosshairs” of its rivals.

“In the event of a war between the US and China over the Taiwan issue, we can infer that China would target US facilities—both military and commercial—located in the Philippines. Our concern is that the US presence in the country is situated within our strategic and critical economic infrastructure,” Tinio said in a statement released on Thursday.

Tinio’s statement followed his heated exchange with Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro during the House committee on appropriations’ hearing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of National Defense last Tuesday, Aug. 25.

During the hearing, Tinio raised reports that US soldiers had attempted to enter the Philippine Veterans Investment Development Corporation Industrial Authority in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental, where the new Philippine Navy dry dock is set to be established.
Teodoro dismissed claims about US interest in the dry dock, saying the presence of foreign troops was for the Balikatan loading exercise.
For Tinio, however, the incident was part of a broader pattern of Washington’s agenda in the country.
He cited the US-led Pax Silica, the US Navy’s use of Subic Bay for repairs and plans for an oil depot in Davao Gulf.

Tinio said the growing US presence in strategic military and economic facilities was particularly concerning because the Philippines lacks the capacity to defend these assets should geopolitical tensions escalate.
“How is the Philippines? The Gulf states are rich countries. They can afford high-tech missile defenses. How are we? What is the capability of the Armed Forces to defend these facilities?” he asked.
Tinio called on the public to remain vigilant against “foreign manipulation and intervention.”
“We must oppose all efforts to sell us out,” he added. /mcm

articles.title: Jellyfish force partial shutdown of French nuclear plant
articles.summary: It is the second consecutive year that jellyfish has forced the closure of the Gravelines power station in northern France.

blocks.text: A massive influx of jellyfish has led to the partial shutdown of a nuclear reactor in northern France.

Two of Gravelines nuclear power station's six units were shut down on Wednesday and Thursday because of the presence of jellyfish in the seawater filtration system, which is used for cooling, Électricité de France (EDF) said.
A third unit has been shut down since 10 August due to the same issue, while a fourth has been closed for an inspection.
Gravelines, one of the country's biggest nuclear power stations located between Dunkirk and Calais in the Hauts-de-France region, was also closed last August because of jellyfish in its filters.
EDF said that units three, four and six were now shut.

Unit three had only been reconnected to the grid on 18 August after the first wave of jellyfish earlier this month, the company said, while units one and two were also operating at reduced power as a preventative measure.
Gravelines' six units each produce 900 megawatts of power. The station is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea.
Several species of jellyfish are native and can be seen around the coast when the waters are warm.
Jellyfish are at their most active in the warmer months. Hot weather increases plankton levels at the water's surface, drawing jellyfish up, experts say.
Measures have been implemented to try to prevent jellyfish infiltration, including a partnership with fishermen who capture and release them further offshore, according to French outlet Ici.
There have been similar issues at other nuclear stations, including at the Torness plant in Scotland in 2011 and Sweden's Oskarshamn plant in 2013, but such cases are rare.

articles.title: We need deeper thinking about video games and violence
articles.summary: Everyone who thinks that video games cause violence is wrong. Everyone who thinks video games have nothing to do with violence is wrong. Before I proceed, I will set forward the idea that any school…

blocks.text: Everyone who thinks that video games cause violence is wrong.
Everyone who thinks video games have nothing to do with violence is wrong.

Before I proceed, I will set forward the idea that any school shooting, any kind of attack like this is tragic and unacceptable and we need to do things as a society to ensure that we are doing everything that we can, not just to prevent them, but providing care and concern so that no one even thinks about doing this to other people.
But I want to focus on technology and tech policy, and to look at the kinds of arguments we are having, and the ones that we should be having.
Knee jerk responses

In what might be considered knee-jerk response, DILG Sec. Jonvic Remulla called for the banning of first-person games. Similarly, Sen. Robin Padilla is condemning game developers for inspiring school shooters. This isn’t much different from the responses to the tragic school shooting only months ago in Tacloban.

In equal knee jerk response, we have lots of people saying that if it were true that games caused violence, then why isn’t there more violence? I come from the generation that played the first FPS’s, and I’ll be honest that this too has been my gut reaction. The corollary then is, if I and all the people around me who ever played violent games have not done anything, then games have nothing to do with it.
RELATED STORY: DICT blocks GoreBox in Philippines after talks with developer
Here’s what I think each side is getting wrong.

The “video games make people violent” side join a long tradition of moral panics. Just this weekend I was in a board game cafe filled with people playing Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering; these days considered harmless pastimes but when I was younger, we were warned that playing these games would lead us to Satanic rituals. It’s hilarious to watch 90s videos of fundamental preachers warning against the new threat of this Satanic force called Pokémon. I’m old enough that in Catholic School we were warned about the Satanic messages in the music of Led Zeppelin and Queen, which could be revealed by backmasking cassettes.
Moral Panics and Genuine Concerns

The targets of such moral panics have shifted as culture and media have evolved. Whether it was worry over slasher films, punk music and gangsta rap, to Harry Potter and Lord of the Rings, to tabletop and video games, it’s been a move by moralist sides to blame pieces of culture for potential or actual harmful behavior. Looking at it with a broad historical scope, the argument falls apart and gets exposed as, well, silly.

However, it is worth noting that there are some points of concern that have merit. While it’s too much to believe that there are “corrupting forces” in these things, and therefore we must protect our children against them is a stretch, what is worth acknowledging is that they are correct in noting that there are some kinds of media and culture that kids should not be allowed to engage with. There’s a reason for ratings systems, age limits, and the like. While those systems and limits will constantly be shifting given societal norms, they are important. You can’t just expose kids to everything and hope for the best.

Which brings us to what the “I’ve played video games and I haven’t shot anybody” side gets wrong. Those of us who lived through the moral panics against Diablo, Mortal Kombat, and Counter-Strike came up in a world with a very different gaming culture. We trash-talked people in front of us (or beside us, trying to keep our spot as challengers stepped up and dropped coins), played in rooms connected via LAN. These days, we aren’t playing inside of the same kinds of games, and if we are, there are rooms that are separate from our experiences.
Games are so different now

This is to acknowledge that the worlds inside of video games today and the experience of games is so different. The scale of the social aspects of games is drastically different from what past generations experienced. We might have been the first to inhabit the MMO worlds of Ragnarok: Online or World of Warcraft, but the social aspects of games like Fortnite and Roblox are something else.

What we get wrong is that when someone says something against video games, they might be getting something right. Broadly video games don’t cause violence. However, it cannot be denied that video game spaces are spaces where sexual predation and radicalization can occur. The games themselves might not be designed as vectors for spreading violent and radical thinking, or as a space for predators to take advantage of children. But that doesn’t mean that bad actors aren’t using the social aspects of those games to do things that were never in the game’s original plans.

Some might want to shift the blame to parents. This interview with a game developer who worked on Roblox encourages parents to be watching their kids “24/7” if they are on Roblox. One can imagine the world of content just twenty years ago, movies had age minimums, video rental stores had sections with the movies marked for age, and in general we had a sense of where kids could go and what kind of things they were exposed to. But now, kids can log on and they have access, and also become accessible, to content and individuals that their parents would have no way to watch let alone control. (Also, what kind of life would it be if every movement done by young people was done under the surveillance of their parents? A different issue entirely, but something worth thinking about as we think about giving parents more control and shifting more responsibility to them.)

Very clearly parents need to play a part in watching what their kids are exposed to. But parental guidance is not enough, and so there needs to be a whole of society approach to this. We need our regulators to actually be regulating the right things. Rather than asking for blanket bans on FPS games, we should be asking our regulators to set expectations on platforms that host games.
You wouldn’t leave kids in an arcade

I will try and make a simple analogy here. If I were running an arcade which allowed small kids to play certain games, then I should be expected to not put extremely violent games or sexual games within access of those small kids. Maybe I need to have a separate room for those games–I’m allowed to offer them and to let age-appropriate people play the games. More importantly, if there are creepers who are trying to isolate young children or radicalize troubled teens, then I should have a responsibility to protect those kids. Even better, I should have a connection with regulators so I know who to report them to.

But what the analogy shows is that it isn’t just parents, or platforms, or regulators, but everyone working together to address this at the various layers. Games and all other content should have some kind of recommendations or verification limits (if you are playing on Steam you run into these all the time).

To the best of their ability, parents should help guide their children’s online behavior. To continue the arcade metaphor, you don’t just drop them off and hope for the best. If they are small you go and join them, if they are older, then you decide how much you can trust them. But then the platform has to step in. Once a parent trusts a platform enough to allow their children to use it, then the platform has a duty of care to the child. And beyond that, we do need regulation that holds platforms accountable.

It’s not just banning video games. And it’s not that video games have nothing to do with violence. We need to be talking more deeply and exploring in a more thoughtful way what we can do here. I know that I might be talking about an internet that doesn’t exist anymore, given the levels of danger and toxicity we see in so many platforms. But I still think people can turn to online games to discover their people, have great experiences, and enrich their lives.

Parents need to provide support for their kids and help them through what they can and should be playing. Platforms need to provide great spaces where kids can have fun, safe experiences. And regulators need to provide frameworks for platforms to adhere to and establish what the bounds are to hold them accountable. It’s going to take a lot more than blanket bans to get us to a better, safer place.

articles.title: Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions
articles.summary: Nickolay Mladenov warns that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.

blocks.text: A senior official on US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas.
Nickolay Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.
He was speaking to the UN Security Council after Israel rejected the 15-point roadmap for Hamas's disarmament, which was announced by the Board of Peace last month.
Hamas has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal. But Israel has insisted that the group must fully disarm before any pullout.

At least 1,303 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed in Palestinian attacks in Gaza over the same period.

The Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza told the Security Council on Wednesday that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed at their last meeting on a mechanism through which his government's remaining questions would be settled and that committees had been established for that purpose.
Mladenov said that process had not stalled but warned that risks remained, including the continued killing of Palestinian civilians in Israeli strikes.

"A ceasefire in fact under which civilians are still buried is not yet one that the people of Gaza can really feel. Every use of force that does not answer an immediate threat, and every incident that the deconfliction mechanism was not asked to resolve, costs this process something very hard to buy back," he added.
Mladenov acknowledged that Hamas too had yet to meet fully its commitment to cease all military activities.
"Every weapon carried, every tunnel still worked and every convoy still obstructed sets the process back and hands an argument to those who want to resume war," he said.

He repeated that under the new roadmap, Israeli troop withdrawal from Gaza "follows verified decommissioning" of Hamas weapons handed over to the Palestinian technocratic committee that will govern Gaza under the Board of Peace's supervision.
"It is sequenced and reciprocal," he said.
That is a key difference from comments made by President Trump's envoy, Jared Kushner, after meeting Israel's prime minister two weeks ago.
He said Israeli withdrawal would be discussed only once the demilitarisation of Gaza was "done" - appearing to change the plan in line with Israel's demands.

Israel's representative told the Security Council meeting that it was committed to last October's US-brokered plan for ending the Gaza war, but she insisted it could not succeed while Hamas still had weapons, tunnels and other military infrastructure.
"Disarmament must come first," she stated.
The Palestinian representative said Israel was killing Palestinian civilians with impunity in Gaza and called on the international community to protect them without delay.

Mladenov warned that if the ceasefire was allowed to collapse, "there will be no roadmap to return to, there will be no administration to deploy, and there will be nothing left of the ground to rebuild".
"That would not be a setback. It would be a point of no return for everyone."
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,430 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

articles.title: Economic team pushes for faster procurement, project implementation
articles.summary: MANILA – The country’s economic team is pushing for faster procurement and implementation of government projects and programs to deliver tangible benefits to Filipinos. During a briefing with the…

blocks.caption: PROPOSED 2027 NEP. Committee on finance briefing on the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program at the Senate of the Philippines in Pasay City on Thursday (Aug. 27, 2026). The Development Budget Coordination Committee presented the proposed national budget and fiscal plans for the coming year,…

blocks.text: MANILA – The country’s economic team is pushing for faster procurement and implementation of government projects and programs to deliver tangible benefits to Filipinos.

During a briefing with the Senate Committee on Finance on the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) on Thursday, Department of Budget and Management (DBM) Acting Secretary Kim Robert de Leon said the government is committed to accelerating infrastructure projects while strengthening safeguards for fund utilization.
De Leon assured lawmakers that infrastructure spending would be accelerated without compromising the budgeting, procurement, accounting and auditing safeguards designed to protect public funds.

“We are not proposing any relaxation of safeguards. In fact, we want more safeguards,” he said when asked whether controls on the audit and validation of infrastructure projects would be eased to speed up government spending.
“What we are looking at is how we can hasten implementation and procurement. The issue is not the safeguards. We need to implement. We have to start implementing,” De Leon added.
De Leon said this as he cited delays in the procurement, awarding and implementation of already-funded infrastructure projects as among the immediate challenges the government must address.

He said the government’s economic managers are working toward a recovery in infrastructure activity beginning in the third quarter of 2026, noting that the DBM has already made available the allotments the Department of Public Works and Highways needs to move forward with its projects.
He said the objective is not simply to spend more or faster, but to ensure appropriated funds translate into “well-planned, properly implemented, and beneficial infrastructure projects.”
Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DepDev) Secretary Arsenio M. Balisacan emphasized the need to fast-track implementation and translate reforms into concrete outcomes.

“Our direction remains anchored in the Philippine Development Plan. Over the administration’s final two years, the focus is an accelerating execution, resolving implementation bottlenecks, and translating reforms into concrete results,” Balisacan said.
Finance Secretary Finance Go vowed responsible fiscal management through stronger revenues, prudent expenditure management and fiscal buffers against future shocks.
He also ensured that government resources must be directed toward investments that generate jobs and create lasting economic value.

“Our national budget can work harder if we invest in programs and projects that can help shape our future. We must look beyond the present and invest in high multiplier programs and projects that create lasting economic value, those that create jobs,” he said. (PNA)

articles.title: Habagat rains to persist as LPA monitored – Pagasa
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon or “habagat” will continue to affect the country, while a low-pressure area (LPA) east of extreme Northern Luzon is not expected to develop into a tropical…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon or “habagat” will continue to affect the country, while a low-pressure area (LPA) east of extreme Northern Luzon is not expected to develop into a tropical cyclone within the next 24 hours, the state weather bureau said Thursday.

In a 5 p.m. weather advisory, Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) weather specialist John Manalo said the LPA was located 850 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon and remained within the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR).
More rain
The “habagat” will bring cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms to Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, Western Visayas, and Negros Island.
Meanwhile, occasional rains are also expected to prevail in Benguet, La Union, Pangasinan, Zambales, Bataan, and Occidental Mindoro due to the enhanced “habagat.”
The rest of the country may experience partly cloudy to cloudy skies with localized thunderstorms, according to Pagasa.
The weather bureau reported that around 100 to 200 millimeters (mm) of rain may affect Benguet, Zambales, and Occidental Mindoro on Friday.

Around 50 to 100 mm are also projected to prevail over Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Bataan, Pampanga, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Antique.
LPA alert
Manalo explained that beyond the 24-hour period, the LPA will have a higher chance of developing into a storm.

“Ibig sabihin, sa susunod na bente kwatro oras, hindi pa natin nakikita na maging isang ganap na bagyo. Pero beyond that period ay mas tataas na ang tsansa na ito ay maging isang ganap na bagyo,” Manalo said.
(This means that within the next 24 hours, we do not yet foresee it developing into a storm. However, beyond that period, the likelihood of it becoming a storm will increase.)
“And kapag naka-high na po ito sa susunod na 24 oras ay magiging bagyo na po itong low-pressure area na minomonitor natin na tatawagin po nating Pilandok,” he added.
(And once it intensifies, within the next 24 hours, the low-pressure area we are monitoring will develop into a tropical cyclone, which we will be named Pilandok.) /gsg

articles.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream pledges no price increase as Ontario company shifts away from U.S. suppliers
articles.summary: Ontario company Chapman’s Ice Cream says it's moving to replace more than 70 per cent of its ingredients from the U.S. by mid-2027, promising no price increases until March 2028.

image.caption: Chapman’s Ice Cream, based in southwestern Ontario, says it is moving to replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients by mid-2027, promising no price increases until March 2028. (CBC )

blocks.text: London
Ontario company Chapman’s Ice Cream says it's moving to replace more than 70 per cent of its ingredients from the U.S. by mid-2027, promising no price increases until March 2028.
Company says it will replace 70% of U.S. ingredients with Canadian, other suppliers by 2027
