blocks.caption: Chapman’s Ice Cream, based in southwestern Ontario, says it is moving to replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients by mid-2027, promising no price increases until March 2028. (CBC )

blocks.text: An Ontario ice cream company says it will replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and won't increase prices for two years.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is shifting away from American suppliers as the trade dispute between Canada and the United States continues. The family-owned company also says it won't raise prices for its ice cream until March 2028.
It began looking for alternatives to U.S. suppliers in March 2025, when the first round of tariffs from the Trump administration was announced, CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“We made a statement at that time that we weren’t raising prices and we were going to start this journey. And here we are. We have not been sitting idle. We have been working very hard,” Chapman told CBC's London Morning on Thursday.
The company said it's on track to replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and components with Canadian or non-U.S. sources by mid-2027.

items: The art of inflicting pain: How to select targets for Canada's counter-tariffs

blocks.text: The sweet move to Ontario sugar cone company
One of the biggest changes involves sugar cones.
There are no producers of industrial sugar cones in Canada, so the company partnered with Original Foods, a Dunville, Ont.-based company, to bring in a cone oven, Chapman said.
“We are going to be the only company in Canada who has a 100 per cent Canadian cone line."
Original Foods Limited will produce the sugar cones for Chapman's. The manufacturer tapped the ice cream retailer a few months ago when trade talks with Canada and the U.S. intensified.

"We knew there will be opportunities for customers who are currently buying in the U.S. to look for local manufacturing and we approached Chapman's to discuss if they would be interested to buy locally," said president Steeve Tremblay.

"It's very rewarding to keep the jobs in Canada. It makes our economy stronger and we're not being dependent outside the country, especially when there's a country that tries to make our economy and our lives more difficult. It's nice to see that we can collaborate and give somewhat of strategic response that’s good for Canada."

The two companies have already signed their agreement and equipment has been purchased in Germany. However, Tremblay said, there have been delays due to Canada's electricity registration requirements and other red tape.

"Sometimes [the requirements] are really unique to Canada and not aligned with European manufacturers, so it causes extra costs and delays and is a perfect example of something that can be reviewed," he said.
Tremblay said he plans to contact other Canadian companies to encourage more local partnerships.
Chapman's is also moving production of wafers used in its ice cream sandwiches to Canada, and is sourcing ingredients such as almonds from Australia and cherries from Chile.

blocks.caption: Ashley Chapman, CEO of Chapman's Ice Cream, says trade dispute between Canada and the U.S. has prompted Canadian companies like Chapman's to reconsider what they produce domestically. (Chapman's Ice Cream)

blocks.text: The trade dispute has prompted Canadian companies like Chapman's to reconsider what they produce domestically, he said.

“The first round last year of tariffs really opened the eyes of a lot of industry in Canada. Companies that we’ve known for years that would never consider producing certain products, suddenly they were saying, 'You know what, maybe we should look at this.'”
He said some of the changes have also proved to be more affordable than expected.

“It’s crazy what this has done for businesses in this country. Almonds from Australia, are you crazy? How is that possible that we could get an even better price, plus freight, from Australia instead of the United States? So we’re finding a lot of opportunities out there.”

items: Consumers say 'resolve is strengthened' to buy Canadian, bringing patriotic shopping movement back to life

blocks.text: Chapman said some of the changes are long-term commitments, including the five-year contract for Canadian-made cones.
Chapman’s is also working to make its production more efficient to help control costs, he added.
“I am fully confident that we are going to make it to the other side of this."
The company said it will continue to use 100 per cent Canadian dairy in its ice cream.

articles.title: Quebec party leaders make their pitches as election campaign kicks off

image.caption: Éric Duhaime, the leader of Conservative Party of Quebec, speaking during today's news conference. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

items: August 27That's a wrap — for nowThe election period is officially underway and all five leaders of Quebec's main political parties have made their initial pitch. As leaders tour the province, you can expect them to release their party platforms and announce campaign promises in the coming weeks.In the meantime, try out CBC's Vote Compass to see which party aligns most with your views.

60,000 workers needed for upcoming electionBenjamin ShinglerWith the election campaign now underway, Élections Québec says it faces a major challenge: recruiting enough staff to run the polls.In a statement to CBC News, the agency confirmed it needs to hire and train more than 60,000 people across the province ahead of the advanced polls and Oct. 5 vote.The agency noted that staffing is an issue leading into every election, adding that an advertising campaign is already underway and applications are open online. The statement stressed that teenagers aged 16 and 17 are eligible to work during the campaign and can learn more about how elections work in the process.

‘I’m the only leader,’ Milliard tells voterMélissa FrançoisThe leader of the Quebec Liberals stopped for an ice cream in the municipality of Batiscan in the Mauricie region. He chose a vanilla and chocolate twist. During the stop, a man approached him and said, “Please get rid of Pablo Rodriguez!” Milliard replied, “I’m the only leader.” Rodriguez, the former leader of the Quebec Liberals, stepped down last December after controversies involving him and his party.

Duhaime's message to Quebec anglophonesHolly CabreraÉric Duhaime, the leader of Conservative Party of Quebec, speaking during today's news conference. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)The PCQ leader had a message to the province's English speakers: "The English community in Quebec has been hostage to the Liberals forever." Duhaime pointed to polls that suggest the Quebec Liberals have lost popularity among francophones.He said that hopefully anglophones realize that they would be better off with Conservative MNAs.

Quebec's economic model is at the ‘end of its rope,’ Duhaime saysHolly CabreraThe PCQ leader said that in the next few hours he would announce the "greatest" tax reduction. He also accused Fréchette of instrumentalizing the tariff war during the election and called her a protectionist. "This election, I want to fight for Quebecers and get more money in their pockets," Duhaime said. "Quebecers aren't fools. They know our [economic] model is not viable," Duhaime said, noting that the model is at the "end of its rope."

Quebec's prosperity shouldn't rely on the U.S., Duhaime saysHolly CabreraÉric Duhaime, the leader of Conservative Party of Quebec, speaks during a news conference, in Sainte-Claire, Que., on Thursday. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)Speaking to Quebecers who are "tired of turning in circles," Duhaime said his party wants to be the "true alternative" to the province's old parties. He said he wants to remove interprovincial barriers to lessen Quebec's reliance on the United States."It's not up to Americans to determine our prosperity. It's up to us. Only us, in Quebec," Duhaime said.

Sole Conservative MNA introduces DuhaimeHolly CabreraBefore Duhaime steps up to the podium, Maïté Blanchette Vézina — the Conservatives’ only MNA — took some time to promote her party's ambitions. "If we're doing politics, it's first and foremost to represent real people," said Blanchette Vézina , who used to be a member of the CAQ. She said the Conservatives have "pragmatic and courageous" solutions for Quebecers.

Duhaime is speaking in BellechasseKwabena OduroÉric Duhaime's campaign bus. (Kwabena Oduro/CBC)The Conservative Party of Quebec leader Éric Duhaime is speaking at a news conference in the riding of Bellechasse, where he is hoping to win a seat. The party is holding an event that started at 5 p.m. to officially launch the party’s campaign. During the campaign, the Conservatives will focus on the cost of living, health care, housing and the autonomy of Quebec and its regions.

Conservative leader feeling ‘confident’Kwabena Oduro3 questions with the leader of the Quebec ConservativesOn the first day of the campaign, CBC's Kwabena Oduro caught up and had a brief chat with Éric Duhaime, the leader of the Conservative Party of Quebec.I just had a quick chat with Éric Duhaime. He says he's feeling confident about his campaign. Duhaime says his team has been preparing for this for the last four years and he's feeling more ready than he was four years ago.He is looking to get a seat at the National Assembly for the first time.He's running in the riding of Bellechasse, just south of Quebec City – one of a few areas where he is hoping his party will make gains.

Montreal mayor’s wish list for next Quebec governmentHénia Ould-HammouMontreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada laid out her requests from the next Quebec government on Wednesday. (Ivanoh Demers/Radio-Canada)Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada outlined her expectations for the next Quebec government at a news conference on Wednesday. Her requests focus on three key points: homelessness and housing, infrastructure and mobility, and public safety. She called on the next government to allocate recurring funding for 3,200 emergency shelter spots and to create three centres specializing in mental health and addiction by the summer of 2027. She reiterated her calls for a REM light-rail train system in the eastern part of the city.She also called for more funding to help with policing and youth violence prevention. Last week, Martinez Ferrada announced that she was moving forward with her plan to gradually equip the city's police officers with body cameras.She also demanded that Quebec change its approach toward Montreal and that the city be consulted before any decision affecting it is made.

articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Thursday honored Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya during a farewell call at Malacañang and conferred him with the Order of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Thursday honored Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya during a farewell call at Malacañang and conferred him with the Order of Sikatuna, Rank of Datu (Grand Cross), Gold Distinction.
During their meeting, Marcos thanked the Japanese envoy for his contributions to strengthening the Philippines’ relationship with Japan, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said.
The President recognized Endo for promoting bilateral exchanges and deepening cooperation between the Philippines and Japan in areas of defense, security, and development cooperation.

Meanwhile, the award cited the envoy’s support for initiatives aligned with the Philippines’ priorities in infrastructure, education, transportation, maritime domain awareness, and human resource development.

“Endo was likewise recognized for advancing Japan’s longstanding commitment to peace and development in Mindanao, including its support for the peace process, grassroots development and the transition of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao,” the PCO said.

“The citation also highlighted the ambassador’s efforts to mobilize humanitarian and development assistance from the Japanese government during natural disasters and recent regional crises,” it added.
Additionally, Marcos acknowledged Endo’s initiatives that fostered friendship, mutual understanding, and goodwill between the Filipino and Japanese peoples.
The Order of Sikatuna is conferred upon individuals who have rendered exceptional and meritorious service to the Philippines.
The Philippines and Japan are celebrating 70 years of normalized relations this year and 11 years of strengthened strategic partnership since 2015. /gsg

articles.title: Thieves steal Bronze Age artefacts from Spanish museum in four-minute heist
articles.summary: The Treasure of Villena is a unique trove of almost ten kilos of gold, bowls, bottles and bracelets dating back to the Bronze Age.

blocks.text: The operation at Villena Museum was "super fast and super professional", a spokesman for Villena town council said.
The city council said the robbery began with a diversion. Around 05:15 local time (03:15 GMT), the alarms went off at the local sports centre, sending police there first, Spanish media reported.
The museum's alarm then went off around 05:20. It took the thieves just four minutes to sweep through museum and leave the building before officers arrived.
The Mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdán, said the thieves "stole a large part of the treasure," specifically all the gold, El Pais reported.
The museum's collection, which dates back to around 1,000 BC, is mainly gold items, but there are also pieces of silver, iron and amber.
It consists of more than 60 bronze age objects, including 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces.
The town is "devastated," Cerdán said. "They've taken most of the treasure."
"I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, of our wealth," the mayor said.
The collection was discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose María Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena.
The Villena council spokesman insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum.
"All security systems were activated."

The past year has seen a series of raids on European museums. In October 2025, thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris in broad daylight, stealing jewellery worth $102m (£75m) before escaping on scooters, in a heist that took about eight minutes.
Last week, four works "of extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy's culture ministry said.
Earlier this month, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth over $10.4m (£7.6m) which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation museum near Parma.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: First BARMM parliamentary elections
articles.summary: Bookmark and refresh this page for the latest news, photos, videos, and analyses as Rappler closely follows the historic elections

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.
Bookmark and refresh this page for the latest news, photos, videos, and analyses as Rappler closely follows the regional elections.
LATEST UPDATES
10 hours ago
Bangsamoro parties clash over key reforms in first debate

Thirteen political parties faced off in Cotabato on Thursday, August 27, for the first BARMM Parliamentary Elections Debate organized by the Institute for Autonomy and Governance. Held at Notre Dame University, the historic face-off showcased competing platforms for the regional government ahead of the landmark polls.

The debates centered on socioeconomic reforms, service decentralization, and resolving clan feuds or rido. Candidates also clashed over Sulu’s exclusion, electoral integrity, and resisting national government interference.

The event ended with party-list groups signing posters to pledge their commitment to civil society advocacies. This included signing covenants of commitment with Duyog Bangsamoro and the Coalition for Social Accountability and Transparency. – Rappler.com
10 hours ago
Delayed services an injustice to Bangsamoro — Loong

“Sang-ayon tayo sa decentralization kasi bakit natin i-centralize dito kung ang outcome ay kalahati ang nagagastos natin, kung ang outcome ay two years tayong delayed sa implementation. Because that is an injustice to the Bangsamoro people,” said engineer Don Mustapha Loong of the Progresibong Bangsamoro Party.
Loong defended decentralization as a way to make government services more efficient and responsive to communities.
He questioned the value of centralizing services when it results in lower spending outcomes and delays of up to two years in implementation.
Loong called the failure to deliver the gains of the Bangsamoro transition “the greatest injustice that could possibly happen.”
He said the “fruits of the revolution” may already be within reach, yet many Bangsamoro people remain unable to experience their benefits. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.
10 hours ago
Lim urges responsible spending, Kashim hits BARMM failures

“We have to take care of taxpayers’ money. Every family, every working-class family, every month, nakikita nila sa payroll nila, tax withheld. Can you imagine that money could’ve gone to one more sack of rice, one week’s worth of grocery?” said Nur-Ainee Tan Lim Misuari of the Mahardika Party.

Lim called for greater accountability in the use of public funds, pointing to the underutilization of the block grant, limited absorptive capacity, and inefficiency in spending within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
She said the region needs leaders who can restrain themselves, put people first, and use public funds for the Bangsamoro.
“This is a government of failure,” Abdulhussein Kashim of Indigenous, Settles, Sama and Minorities Alliance Party described the situation bluntly.
He said the government has a strong legal foundation to deliver resources to the people but has failed to do so.
Despite the criticisms, Lim said there remains an opportunity for the Bangsamoro to “rise from the ashes,” particularly for undecided voters who are weighing their choices.
She reminded the audience that “our children are watching,” and that the region’s youth continue to dream of a better future. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.
11 hours ago
Sema, Basher clash over national interference in BARMM polls

A tense exchange unfolded between lawyer Omar Yasser Sema of the Bangsamoro Party and Alipikre Basher of the People’s Consultative Party, also known as the Mushawara Party, over electoral reform and possible national government interference in the regional elections.
Sema asked whether Basher would support reforms if interference occurs, clarifying that it was a serious question.
Basher affirmed his commitment to an “honest and credible election,” saying they are “101%” committed to a credible electoral process.
“Hindi ka matatakot sa national government?” Sema asked.
Basher hesitated before cackling in response, drawing attention from the audience. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.
11 hours ago
UBJP, BGC urge more representation for women, PWDs
“Ako po ay isa sa living [examples] of UBJP, kung paano itinaas ng UBJP ang participation ng kababaihan,” said lawyer Sha Elijah Dumama-Alba of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party.
Dumama-Alba highlighted the political participation of women and persons with disabilities as part of the party’s future advocacy.

She cited the Bangsamoro Women Commission, women’s empowerment, political subsidy funds for women candidates, and gender-based audits as pathways to strengthen women’s representation and participation.
Meanwhile, Amir Mawalil of the BARMM Grand Coalition said the coalition wants to work with all political parties and support initiatives that advance inclusion.
Both groups pointed to the Bangsamoro Gender and Development Code and stronger institutional mandates as mechanisms in expanding political participation and representation. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.

blocks.caption: What you need to know about the first BARMM parliamentary elections

blocks.text: 11 hours ago
UBJP backs national transitional justice commission

“Kung gusto nating ma-address ang historical injustices, hindi lamang ito sa Bangsamoro region, kundi sa buong Pilipinas,” said lawyer Sha Elijah Dumama-Alba of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP).
Dumama-Alba called for the establishment of a national transitional justice commission under the national government to address historical injustices and legitimate grievances.
She said lasting peace requires justice, healing, and credible institutions.
As one of the signatories to the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, the UBJP supports strengthening the Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission.
The party calls for adequate funding, technical capacity, and legal and institutional protection, with communities and the ulama included in its implementation and governance. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.
12 hours ago
Bangsamoro groups push for justice-based solutions to rido
“Sinusuportahan natin ang hybrid at restorative justice,” said Amir Mawalil of the BARMM Grand Coalition. Rido is a clan or family feud that can lead to repeated conflict and violence.
Mawalil called for the institutionalization of a dispute resolution framework across the Bangsamoro government, with all agencies helping implement it.
He identified land ownership and loose firearms among the issues that can fuel rido, stressing the need for responsive land distribution and addressing its root causes.
Meanwhile, lawyer Omar Yasser Sema of the Bangsamoro Party argued that the root of rido is not simply land conflict but the failure to address crimes through the justice system.
Sema called for greater access to justice and equal application of the law to prevent conflicts from escalating and recurring. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.
12 hours ago
ABOT, PBB back settlers’ rights, inclusive Bangsamoro
“‘Di po natin sasayangin ang ating nasimulan na interfaith dialogue, kasama na doon ang culture of peace natin,” said Emran Mohammad of the Alliance of Bangsamoro Tri-People’s Party (ABOT).
Mohammad emphasized inclusivity for Moro, indigenous peoples, and settlers, including the concerns of Christian settlers, schools, churches, and other institutions.
He stressed the importance of continuing interfaith dialogue and fostering a culture of peace.

“Kailangan ng pagkakaintindihan at pagkakaunawaan para matamo ang pagkakaisa,” said engineer Addie Unsi of the Partido Bangon Bangsamoro (PBB), who also studied at Notre Dame University alongside Mohammad.
Unsi expressed support for ABOT’s position on recognizing settlers’ rights.
“Ang PBB ay susuportahan po ang posisyon ng ABOT doon sa pagkilala ng karapatan ng settlers,” Unsi said.
He also pledged support for a settlers’ office with a dedicated budget to enable it to carry out its programs. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.
12 hours ago
Progresibong Bangsamoro Party urges open economic zones in Basilan, Tawi-Tawi
“The island region is the front door in terms of economic development,” said engineer Don Mustapha Loong of the Progresibong Bangsamoro Party.
Loong highlighted the strategic position of Basilan and Tawi-Tawi as gateways for economic development in the Bangsamoro.
He said the focus should not only be on smuggling but also on creating a framework for open economic zones and free ports that would maximize the region’s strategic position and resources.
He stressed that despite this advantage, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi have yet to fully benefit from it. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.

articles.title: Man who attacked nun on CCTV in Jerusalem acquitted on grounds of mental health
articles.summary: A Jerusalem court said the Jewish attacker was having a psychotic episode when he assaulted the nun, in an incident which caused outrage.

blocks.text: An Israeli court has acquitted a Jewish man who attacked a nun in Jerusalem, in an incident caught on CCTV which drew widespread condemnation.

Jerusalem Magistrates Court said Yona Schreiber was experiencing a psychotic episode when he pushed over and kicked the French nun in the Old City in occupied East Jerusalem in April. It ruled that he was not criminally responsible for his actions and ordered him to be sent to a psychiatric hospital for up to six years.
Video of the attack caused outrage, and deepened concerns after a rise in harassment of Christian clergy and pilgrims by Jewish extremists in the Old City.
The victim, who hit her head on a stone block, suffered a bruised face and leg.
Schreiber, 36, had been charged with assault motivated by hostility towards a religious group.
According to the district psychiatrist's report, Schreiber "was in a psychotic state at the time of the act and is not substantively fit to stand trial".
The prosecution accepted the psychiatrist's opinion and asked for Schreiber to be acquitted and committed to hospital.
Judge Ofir Tishler said that although Schrieber had attacked the nun, he was ordering his acquittal due to his mental health.
At the time of the attack, the French Consulate in Jerusalem said it strongly condemned Schreiber's "aggression".
The director of the French Biblical and Archaeological School, where the nun is a researcher, called the assault an "act of sectarian violence".

Israel's foreign ministry denounced the attack, calling it a "shameful act [which] stands in direct contradiction to the values of respect, coexistence, and religious freedom upon which Israel is founded and to which it remains deeply committed."

"Israel remains firmly committed to safeguarding freedom of religion and freedom of worship for all faiths, and to ensuring that Jerusalem remains a city where every community can live, pray, and practice its faith in safety and dignity," the ministry said on X.

While the violence of the attack on the nun is unusual, in the past few years in Jerusalem's Old City there have been regular cases of religious Jews spitting and acting aggressively towards those wearing Christian religious dress or symbols.

Church properties have been vandalised and there have also been bitter disputes caused by settler takeovers. Church leaders accuse Israel of trying to change the status quo – long-standing agreements on ownership and responsibilities - at their holy places.

A 2025 report by the Rossing Center, a Jerusalem-based organisation which aims to foster better inter-faith relations in the Holy Land, describes a "recent surge in overt animosity towards Christianity", putting this down to "a continued deepening of polarisation and ultra-nationalist political trends".

articles.title: What caused the Nepal-Tibet flash floods?
articles.summary: At least 270 people have died in the massive flash floods, while more than 800 others are missing.

blocks.text: The US Geological Survey says the floods in the Nepal-Tibet border were triggered by a "glacial collapse" - meaning a glacier or part of a glacier had disintegrated.
Initial reports led authorities to believe that an earthquake had been the cause.
The cause of the glacial collapse has not been determined, but scientists have warned that Himalayan glaciers are melting at an accelerating rate due to rising temperatures and climate change.

articles.title: Death toll at least 359, with more than 1,000 missing in Nepal, Tibet after catastrophic floods

image.caption: Police personnel rescue stranded residents from houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Thursday. (Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Rescuers in Nepal, Tibet race to find flood survivors, including multiple Canadians

Rescue teams searched on Thursday for hundreds of missing people along the Nepal-Tibet border, where a catastrophic and deadly torrent of water and mud several stories high swept through communities a day earlier following a glacier collapse.

Citing authorities in Nepal and China, The Associated Press says more than 390 people have been killed and more than 1,400 others are missing. Reuters says at least 359 people are dead and nearly 1,000 are missing, including the citizens of several countries from around the world, after the flash floods that occurred Wednesday morning local time.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said in a statement the government is "aware of 30 Canadians and permanent residents in Nepal and the Tibet region whose whereabouts and well-being have not yet been confirmed." Though she stressed the number could change given the difficult circumstances on the ground, which have included communication issues.
A relative of Dhaval and Megha Shah said the couple from Port Moody, B.C., are among the missing Canadians.
Nikita Shah, Dhaval's cousin, said the couple was on a "spiritual journey" in Nepal, and the last time they heard from them was Tuesday night.
Shah said the couple was staying at Hotel Kailash.

"We don't know if the infrastructure is still there or not, like we get a lot of misinformation, so it would be very helpful if the Canadian government can help," said Shah. "The Canadian government needs to do something about this."
Global Affairs Canada said in a statement that it is sending five consular officials to Kathmandu to support Canadians and co-ordinate with local officials on the ground.
"In addition to working closely with Nepalese and Chinese counterparts, we are also co-ordinating with international partners and allies who also have citizens in the region," it said.
The Nepal Tourism Board, which has provided numbers of those missing from a number of countries, had earlier said 25 Canadians were among the missing.

blocks.caption: Police personnel rescue stranded residents from houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Thursday. (Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: The region's steep valleys are economic lifelines and travel corridors, but are precarious when disaster strikes. Images showed what appeared to be the second floors of buildings in Nuwakot slathered in mud after the torrent rushed by. Debris hung from tree branches and wires, vehicles were buried and some stunned survivors were caked in mud.

"When I reached Dhunge bazaar, in half an hour, the flood came and damaged all the market. People were preparing to go to the office then," resident Shoyam Rajbhandari said. "How many people are missing or dead, we don't know."
PHOTOS | Before and after the floods:
UN dips into rescue fund

The United Nations' humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, announced Thursday he has ordered the release of $2 million US from the UN's Central Emergency Response Fund to help with medical care, shelter and water.
Fletcher added that emergency teams had been mobilized and additional ones were on standby.

The vast majority of the dead and 826 of the missing were in Nepal, with three dead and 558 missing in Tibet, authorities said. According to Nepal's Tourism Board, 517 of the missing people in the country were foreigners and 178 of them were from India.

items: Flash floods kill more than 160 in Nepal, Tibet
Hundreds of people, including tourists, missing after flood in Nepal

blocks.text: In addition, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Lin Jian said that nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side.
Nepalese officials said that dozens of bridges were destroyed and nearly 40 kilometres of roads were damaged, complicating search efforts.
The Nepalese army has rescued more than 100 people from flood-affected areas through helicopter operations on Thursday morning, army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said.
The science behind Nepal's violent flash flood

At least eight foreign nationals were airlifted to the country's capital, Kathmandu, he said, adding that army teams also rescued people trapped inside facilities linked to the Trishuli hydropower project.
Rescuers found bodies about 100 kilometres downstream from the disaster zone in Chitwan district. Dozens of injured people have been transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care.

Bishal Kumar Bhandari, chairman of the Nepal Red Cross Society, said they have shifted focus from rescue to large-scale relief operations in the flood-hit districts. He said that around 1,200 people were displaced from at least three villages.

In Tibet, a mudslide that struck near the land border crossing of Gyirong Port on Wednesday left mud in the surrounding areas more than 1.5 metres deep on average, with some road sections exceeding two metres, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported. Roads leading to the port were all damaged, while secondary collapses or landslides might occur as rain continued in the area, it added.
Melting glaciers more common
The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) first reported a magnitude 4.4 earthquake early Wednesday, about 66 kilometres north of Kathmandu, near the border.

The USGS later updated its analysis to say the seismic event it measured was a magnitude 5.2 glacier collapse that sent debris flowing downstream with catastrophic impact on communities. It said its determination was based on data from nearby seismic stations, long-period seismic waves and satellite imagery, and that no earthquake had occurred.
Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday's flash flood.

"Hydrological observations indicate the exceptional speed and magnitude of the flood wave," they said in an emailed statement, noting that water levels at one point on the Trishuli river rose by as much as nine metres over half an hour.
The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi, had maximum flooding, they said.
Drone footage shows destructive aftermath of Nepal floods

The steep slopes and the lush valleys below the Himalayan mountain range, which span several Asian countries, are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides. Melting glaciers have become more common because of warming because of human-caused climate change.
Researchers in Kathmandu found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting faster, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000.

blocks.caption: A man who was airlifted from Rasuwa district receives first aid at a mobile hospital staffed by army personnel in Trishuli, in Nuwakot district, Nepal. (Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters)

articles.title: Collapsed glacier likely caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, scientists say
articles.summary: Preliminary investigations by scientists have pointed to a collapsed glacier as the cause, highlighting the issue of rapidly melting Himalayan ice.

blocks.text: Aerial footage shows floods on Nepal-Tibet border

Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier as the cause of the flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, highlighting the issue of rapidly melting Himalayan ice, scientists have told the BBC.
Initial reports of an earthquake led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the flood that has killed at least 389 people.
However, the US Geological Survey then clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates.
The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event.

Dr Simon Cook, a glacier expert with the University of Dundee, told the BBC his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.
He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a northwesterly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.

blocks.caption: BBC graphic showing how a glacier collapse sent ice and rock debris into a river between Tibet and Nepal

blocks.text: An analysis , externalby the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), an intergovernmental scientific institution, found there could have been "an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude area".

This caused a "large volume of ice and rock debris" to enter the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, which in turn generated a sudden surge in the river carrying water, sediment and large boulders downstream.
The centre found that water levels in rivers downstream rose by between seven and nine metres within a span of 30 minutes, and several water monitoring stations were washed away or damaged.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Scientists say a collapsed glacier near the Langtang Lirung peak likely caused the disaster

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Scientists say a collapsed glacier near the Langtang Lirung peak likely caused the disaster
Mike Searle, a professor of earth sciences at Oxford University, said that this whole process - from landslide to flood - could have taken hours or even days.
"The sheer wave of debris suggests there could have been a landslide first; the water built up, dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC.

The topography of the area could have also exacerbated the flood. Searle pointed out that Langtang Lirung sits on the crest of the high Himalayas and there are "incredibly steep valleys" on both sides of the mountain, which could have funnelled the water at higher speeds.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Images from the scene show the steep sides of the affected valley

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Images from the scene show the steep sides of the affected valley
It is still unclear what caused the glacier to collapse on Wednesday.

Searle said that Langtang Lirung, like the rest of the Himalayas, has been slowly rising due to long-term tectonic movement, where one plate has been pushing another plate up. "It's like putting a jack under the car, and then jacking it up."
"As the mountain is rising, the glacier gets steeper and steeper, and it's inevitable that parts of it fall off."

But usually these are smaller chunks which temporarily block the rivers, and are easily flushed out, he said. However, in this disaster, the whole glacier seems to have collapsed "in one go", which Searle said is "very unusual". "These floods happen all the time, but not at this scale."

He said Wednesday's event likely happened because of "two different processes - tectonics with the Himalayas uplifting, and then climate change with increasingly high temperatures and melting of glaciers.
"The whole thing is combining to form these catastrophic disasters that we are now seeing at a regular basis."
Scientists for years have warned of melting ice and permafrost, which is centuries-old frozen soil, in the Himalayas due to climate change.

One analysis released by ICIMOD, external earlier this year found that the Hindu Kush Himalaya glaciers are now losing ice at double the rate since 2000. This in turn exacerbates dangers such as flooding.
Dr Cook pointed out that there have been similar incidents of floods and landslides caused by glacier collapses in India, Switzerland and Italy in recent years.

In 2021, a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people. Scientists later estimated that the impact of the collapse was equivalent to 15 atomic bombs.
Even in Nepal, the same region saw flooding last year caused by a glacial lake in Tibet bursting.

blocks.caption: Aerial images showing a before and after of the Trishuli river on 23 and 26 August. In the second photo, brown sediment can be seen spilling out over the banks.

blocks.text: Mohd Farooq Azam, a specialist with ICIMOD, said the increasing frequency of hazards in the cryosphere - or the frozen parts of the Earth - "is becoming more visible than ever before. The pace of change is so rapid."
While it is difficult to say whether any single event is caused by climate change, "when you look at the pattern of these events, you do think climate change could have an impact," said Dr Cook.

"The logic is that with a warming planet, you will see shrinking glaciers, lots of snow melt. The permafrost that is partially holding some mountainsides together is warming and thawing and degrading."
"So you are going to get more landslides, debris flows, glacial meltwater, lake outbursts, glacier collapses, because climate warming ultimately destabilises these high mountain environments."

articles.title: 'The flood took everything': Nepal survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away
articles.summary: One woman says her father, mother, sister and sister's children were carried away before her eyes.
articles.byline: Shaktimaya Tamang, Shreejana Shrestha, Gabriela Pomeroy

blocks.text: Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud.

At least 389 people have died and 900 others are missing after floods wiped out entire villages on the border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, with a force so powerful seismologists initially identified it as an earthquake.
Rescuers trudged through thick mud and debris on Thursday as Nepalese authorities rushed to bring aid and relief supplies to the affected areas.
"My family members were swept away by the flood in front of my eyes," Kalpana Malla from Nepal's Nuwakot district told the BBC.
Malla said her father, mother, sister and sister's children were all claimed by the disaster.
"They could not escape the flood; there was no chance at all," she said. "This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived but couldn't explain how."
Her son, Sugam Malla, said he saved his mother by pulling her hand.
He said he had given his phone to his sister so she could keep in touch, but the mobile was no longer reachable.
"I am worried she must be swept away."
Another woman, Goma Pandit, said she had lost her buffaloes and all her other cattle.
"My farmland is also swept away. Ten sacks of mustard seeds, tons of corn and rice paddy are all gone. Nothing is left."
At Kathmandu's TU Teaching Hospital, families of those missing in the floods wait anxiously for updates.
Holding up her phone, Ram Khumari Shrestha says: "This is my husband. He was off to Rasuwa as a part of his driving job. He was in contact with me until 8 pm yesterday.
"But I couldn't call him this morning. The phone was switched off," she told the BBC.
Mani Shrestha Bishwa was also camped out at the hospital on Wednesday night, hoping to hear from his younger brother, cousin, uncle and friend.
"I last contacted them at 8:30 in the morning," he said.
Trekking guide Sonam Dorjee missed the flood in his home village of Rasiwa Syafru by about an hour. He had left at 08:00 local time.
As he was driving to Kathmandu, Dorjee told the BBC he had heard the sound of floods gushing into their village.
"It [sounded] like an earthquake," he said. "My house has collapsed... I have seen a photo."
Dorjee said his sister, Dechen Tamang, was missing, along with her husband and several other family members.
He described the flood as "sudden and devastating".
"Many survivors are now left without homes and they need emergency rescue and evacuation, as well as food, temporary accommodation and medical support."
He is praying his sister is found alive. "There is a 10% chance, we hope," he said.

articles.title: Partial lunar eclipse to grace Canadian skies tonight
articles.summary: On the night of Aug. 27-28, a partial lunar eclipse will be visible across the country. Here's when to see it.

image.caption: A partial lunar eclipse will occur on Aug. 27 and 28, and will be seen across most of Canada. (Nicole Mortillaro)

blocks.text: Science
On the night of Aug. 27-28, a partial lunar eclipse will be visible across the country. Here's when to see it.
Lunar eclipse comes 2 weeks after total solar eclipse seen in parts of Europe
Listen to this article
Estimated 3 minutes
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

blocks.caption: A partial lunar eclipse will occur on Aug. 27 and 28, and will be seen across most of Canada. (Nicole Mortillaro)

blocks.text: On the night of Aug. 27-28, a partial lunar eclipse will be visible across the country.
The eclipse comes roughly two weeks after the total solar eclipse that was seen across Iceland, Spain and a small portion of Portugal.
While this will be a partial eclipse, it will be a deep one, with 93 per cent coverage at its maximum.

Lunar eclipses occur when the moon moves through Earth’s shadow, called its umbra. Before it enters the umbra, however, it passes through Earth’s outer, dimmer shadow, called the penumbra. However, because it is much dimmer, it’s difficult to see with the naked eye when this occurs.

blocks.caption: This illustration shows the movement of the moon through Earth's shadow for the Aug. 27-28 partial eclipse. (Sky &Telescope)

blocks.text: Most of Canada will see the entire duration of the eclipse, while Western Canada will see the partial eclipse already taking place as the moon rises.

items: NASA says it will put humans on the surface of the moon in 2028. How realistic is that?
The International Space Station is old and leaky. Should it be decommissioned sooner rather than later?

blocks.text: The great news is that, unlike with a solar eclipse, you don’t need any protective eyewear to watch the event.
Also unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse takes place over hours, not minutes.

blocks.caption: All (or most) of the lunar eclipse on August 27-28 will be viewable across North and South America. (Leah Tiscione/Sky & Telescope)

blocks.text: When to see it
The eclipse will begin as the moon enters Earth’s penumbra at roughly 10 p.m. ET, but that’s not when you want to go out to start observing.

Instead, the visible part of the eclipse begins at 10:33 p.m. ET on Aug. 27 and ends at 1:52 a.m. on Aug. 28. The deepest part of the eclipse will occur at 12:13 a.m. with almost all of the moon appearing darkened.
This is just one of many astronomical events taking place this month.

"It's kind of a fun one because … August had so many great things going on for it and still does," said Elaina Hyde, director of the Allan I. Carswell Observatory York University’s department of physics and astronomy in Toronto.

"We had, of course, the very, very partial solar eclipse back on August 12th. We had the Perseids, which were either fabulous or slightly less fabulous, depending on how cloudy your skies were. And, of course, the Jupiter-Mercury conjunction."
Will it be a "blood moon"?
"It's a partial eclipse, so it's not going to turn 100 per cent red, but depending on where you are in Canada, it will still be pretty red," Hyde said.
The great thing about lunar eclipses is that there's no need for any equipment — just your eyes.
"This is a naked eye object, but if you have binoculars or a small telescope or just a [cellphone] camera with a really good night mode, you should be able to get pretty good pictures," Hyde said.

articles.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America'

image.caption: A map labelling Lake Ontario as 'Lake America' is seen behind U.S. President Donald Trump as he speaks in the Oval Office of the White House on Thursday. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" as tensions with Canada worsen.
Carney pushes back on move, says Canadians will call it Lake Ontario 'now and always'
Listen to this article
Estimated 4 minutes
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.
Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" as tensions with Canada worsen.
Sitting near a map with the name "Lake America" over the body of water, Trump said "entitled" Canada has been difficult to deal with and repeated claims the country was ripping off the United States.
"They want to be treated like a state, but they are not a state," Trump said.
When asked why he was targeting American allies with these types of actions instead of American adversaries, Trump said, "they haven't treated us well."
"The Canadian officials have treated us very badly," Trump said. "They are nasty people."

blocks.caption: A map labelling Lake Ontario as 'Lake America' is seen behind U.S. President Donald Trump as he speaks in the Oval Office of the White House on Thursday. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade negotiations fell apart on Friday. Both countries have accused each other of implementing 11th-hour changes.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the agreement became untenable. The federal government unveiled its retaliatory measures, set to go in place on Sept. 8.

items: Trump's top trade negotiator disputes Canadian assertion that U.S. made last-minute demands

blocks.text: Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario Premier Doug Ford.
The two exchanged insults, with Ford calling the president a bully, among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a "less charismatic, intelligent" version of his late brother, Rob.

blocks.caption: Boats float on Lake Ontario Tuesday with Toronto's skyline seen in the background. (Adrian Kraus/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum — who previously was governor of border state North Dakota — posted on social media "the places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States."
He said he's proud to enact the name change.
'Real foolishness'
In Canada, the move prompted incredulity by officials on social media.
Carney said Canadians will call the body of water Lake Ontario "now and always," while Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said "we're into some real foolishness now."
"It's Lake Ontario, buddy," Houston said.
At an unrelated news conference in Winnipeg, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew described the situation as an over-the-hill rock star playing old hits at a casino.
"I think that's the part of Donald Trump's presidency we're at now," Kinew said.

"He thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie with the Gulf of Mexico, and he's trying to bring back that, and he's trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it's a little sad and it's not his best work."
Where Trump’s trade war with Canada could backfire | About That
Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes — is located between Ontario and New York. The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
The lake's name comes from the Huron Indigenous people's word "oniatarí:io," which means "lake of shining waters."
Carney said on social media that the name is more than 400 years old, and predates both Canada and the U.S. as countries.
Gulf of Mexico saga
Last year, Trump signed an executive order to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
It only applies to U.S. federal documents and geographic services, but some online map services also made the change.

items: 'Gulf of America' shift won't be the first time Google Maps has changed names depending on your location

blocks.text: The geographic controversy led to the White House removing The Associated Press from certain duties covering the president after the news service did not use "Gulf of America" in its reporting.

The Associated Press took the White House to court in a dust-up that led to Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ripping many authorities away from the White House Correspondents' Association, the organization of journalists who cover the president.
